\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{MAXNUM}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Q})\COLON \mathbb{Q}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{MINNUM}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Q})\COLON \mathbb{Q}}}

The operators \OPR{MAX} and \OPR{MAXNUM} return whichever argument is larger
in the total order defined by \EXP{<}, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{=}, \EXP{\geq}, \EXP{>}, and \OPR{CMP},
and the operators \OPR{MIN} and \OPR{MINNUM} return whichever argument is smaller.
(For all four, if the arguments are equal, then the result equals that same value.)

The operators \OPR{MAXNUM} and \OPR{MINNUM} differ from
\OPR{MAX} and \OPR{MIN} in their treatment of \EXP{0/0}:
if one argument is \EXP{0/0} and the other is not, then \OPR{MAX} or \OPR{MIN} returns \EXP{0/0} but
\OPR{MAXNUM} or \OPR{MINNUM} returns the argument that is not \EXP{0/0}.


%  opr |self| : QQ
\Method{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \left|\mathord{\KWD{self}}\right| \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \mathbb{Q}}}

The absolute value operator \EXP{\left|\ldots\right|} returns the negative of this rational number
if the argument is less than zero, and otherwise returns the argument.

The absolute value of \EXP{0/0} is \EXP{0/0}.


%  signum(self): ZZ
\Method{\EXP{\VAR{signum}(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}

The method \VAR{signum} returns \EXP{-1} if this rational number is less than zero,
\EXP{0} if this rational number is zero, and \EXP{1} if this rational number is greater than zero.

The signum of \EXP{0/0} is \EXP{0/0}.


%  numerator(self): ZZ
%  denominator(self): ZZ
\Method{\EXP{\VAR{numerator}(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\VAR{denominator}(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}

The method \VAR{numerator} returns the numerator of this rational number,
and the method \VAR{denominator} returns the denominator of this rational number,
when this rational number is represented in lowest terms (such that the greatest common divisor
of numerator and denominator is 1).

The numerator of \EXP{+\infty} is \EXP{1},
the numerator of \EXP{-\infty} is \EXP{-1},
and the numerator of \EXP{0/0} is \EXP{0};
the denominator of \EXP{+\infty}, \EXP{-\infty}, or \EXP{0/0} is \EXP{0}.


%  floor(self): ZZ
%  opr LF self RF: ZZ
%  ceiling(self): ZZ
%  opr LC self RC: ZZ
%  truncate(self): ZZ
%  round(self): ZZ
\Method{\EXP{\VAR{floor}(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \lfloor \mathord{\KWD{self}} \rfloor\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\VAR{ceiling}(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\KWD{opr} \lceil \mathord{\KWD{self}} \rceil\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\VAR{round}(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}
\Method*{\EXP{\VAR{truncate}(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Z}}}

The method \VAR{floor}, likewise the enclosing operator \EXP{\lfloor\ldots\rfloor},
returns the largest integer that is not greater than this rational number.

The method \VAR{ceiling}, likewise the enclosing operator \EXP{\lceil\ldots\rceil},
returns the smallest integer that is not less than this rational number.

The method \VAR{round} returns the integer that is closest to this rational number,
but if this rational number is exactly halfway between two consecutive integers,
then \VAR{round} returns whichever of the two integers is even.

The method \VAR{truncate} returns the ceiling of this rational number if it is
negative, and otherwise returns the floor of this rational number.
(This has the effect of taking the floor of the magnitude, also called
``rounding toward zero.'')

All of these methods throw a \TYP{DivisionByZero} if this rational number is
\EXP{+\infty}, \EXP{-\infty}, or \EXP{0/0}, none of which has an integer value;
so does a division by zero whose result is an integer (\chapref{operators}).
\revision{revival-rational-rounding}{Before this revision the sentence said that
all of these methods simply return the argument if it is \EXP{+\infty},
\EXP{-\infty}, or \EXP{0/0}, a rational number where the entries above declare
an integer result. It now says that they throw a \TYP{DivisionByZero} there, as
\library\ do.}

numerator(self): ZZ
    denominator(self): ZZ  (* Ideally would be NN *)
    opr |self| : QQ = |numerator(self)| / denominator(self)
    (* Note that 0/0 = 0/0 is supposed to be true (//unlike// the behavior of floating-point NaN) *)
    opr =(self, other:QQ):Boolean =
        numerator(self) = numerator(other) AND: denominator(self) = denominator(other)
    opr =/=(self, other:QQ):Boolean = NOT (self = other)
    opr <(self, other:QQ):Boolean = do
        (a, b) = (numerator(self), denominator(self))
        (c, d) = (numerator(other), denominator(other))
        (b=0 AND d=0 AND a=-1 AND c=1) OR (a d < b c)
    end
    opr <=(self, other:QQ):Boolean = (self < other) OR (self = other)
    opr >(self, other:QQ):Boolean = (other < self)
    opr >=(self, other:QQ):Boolean = (other <= self)
    (** In case of 0/0, %MIN% and %MAX% return 0/0, otherwise it respects the
        total order. **)
    opr MIN(self, other:QQ):QQ =
        if self < other then self elif other < self then other elif other = 0/0 then other else self end
    opr MAX(self, other:QQ):QQ =
        if self > other then self elif other > self then other elif self = 0/0 then self else other end
    opr MINMAX(self, other:QQ):(QQ,QQ) =
        if self > other then (other,self)
        elif other > self then (self,other)
        elif other=0/0 then (other,other)
        elif self=0/0 then (self,self)
        else (self,other) end

    opr -(self):QQ = (-numerator(self)) / denominator(self)
    opr +(self,other:QQ):QQ =
        if self = other AND denominator(self) = 0 then self else
            (a, b) = (numerator(self), denominator(self))
            (c, d) = (numerator(other), denominator(other))
            (a d + b c) / b d
        end
    opr -(self,other:QQ):QQ = self + (-other)
    opr DOT(self,other:QQ):QQ = do
        (a, b) = (numerator(self), denominator(self))
        (c, d) = (numerator(other), denominator(other))
        a c / b d
    end
    opr TIMES(self,other:QQ):QQ = self DOT other
    opr juxtaposition (self,other:QQ):QQ = self DOT other
    opr /(self,other:QQ):QQ = do
        (a, b) = (numerator(self), denominator(self))
        (c, d) = (numerator(other), denominator(other))
        a d / b c
    end
    opr ^(self, other:AnyIntegral):QQ =
        if -other > 0 then   (* Way too clever by half (to avoid infinite recursion on 2^(-63)) *)
            (denominator(self)/numerator(self))^(-other)
        else
            (numerator(self))^other / (denominator(self))^other
        end
    floor(self):ZZ = if self < 0 then -ceiling(-self) else truncate(self) end
    opr |\self/| : ZZ = floor(self)
    ceiling(self):ZZ = if denominator(self) = 0 then throw DivisionByZero else
        (a, b) = (numerator(self), denominator(self))
        if a < 0 then -floor(-self) else (a + b - 1) DIV b end
    end
    opr |/self\| : ZZ = ceiling(self)
    truncate(self):ZZ = if denominator(self) = 0 then throw DivisionByZero else numerator(self) DIV denominator(self) end
    round(self): ZZ = do x = self + 1/2; z = floor(x); if z = x AND odd z then z-1 else z end end
    opr MINNUM(self, other:QQ):QQ =
        if self < other then self elif other < self then other elif self = 0/0 then other else self end
    opr MAXNUM(self, other:QQ):QQ =
        if self > other then self elif other > self then other elif self = 0/0 then other else self end
end

object Ratio(num: ZZ, den: ZZ) extends { QQ }
    getter asString(): String = if den = 1 then num.asString else num.asString || "/" || den.asString end
    getter isNaN(): Boolean = (numerator(self) = 0 AND denominator(self) = 0)
    getter isInfinite(): Boolean = (numerator(self) =/= 0 AND denominator(self) = 0)
    (* note: The following will be wrong if num is very large but
    comparable in magnitude to den.  Good algorithms for this case
    exist (we can find the simplest rational within epsilon of the
    given rational) and we ought to support them. *)
    asFloat(self): RR64 = asFloat(num) / asFloat(den)
    numerator(self):ZZ = num
    denominator(self):ZZ = den
end

trait AnyIntegral extends { Number } comprises { ZZ, ZZ64, ZZ32, NN64, NN32 }

diff --git a/Specification/appendices/changes.tex b/Specification/appendices/changes.tex
index 412aea4fc..372e2b26e 100644
--- a/Specification/appendices/changes.tex
+++ b/Specification/appendices/changes.tex
@@ -3022,6 +3022,62 @@ Empty bodies are ignored.
 \item[Route C] The same under route~C.
 \end{description}
 
+\subsection{The rounding of an infinite or indefinite rational}
+\seclabel{revival-rational-rounding}
+
+\begin{description}
+\item[Affected section] \secref{basic-rationals}.
+\item[Change] The sentence after the method entries of \VAR{floor}, \VAR{ceiling},
+\VAR{round} and \VAR{truncate} and of the enclosing operators
+\EXP{\lfloor\ldots\rfloor} and \EXP{\lceil\ldots\rceil} said that all of these
+methods simply return the argument if it is \EXP{+\infty}, \EXP{-\infty}, or
+\EXP{0/0}; it now says that they throw a \TYP{DivisionByZero} there, none of
+these values having an integer value, as a division by zero whose result is an
+integer does (\chapref{operators}).
+The entries' result type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} is unchanged.
+The sentence's opening words, ``For types \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and
+\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}},'', left it before (\secref{revival-rationals}).
+\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
+revival's decision of 9~October 2026 that the declared integer result and the
+peers win over the sentence.
+The method entries declare the result \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, and \library\ declare
+it too; a method that returned its argument at \EXP{+\infty}, \EXP{-\infty} or
+\EXP{0/0} returned a rational number where it declares an integer, and the
+compiled type checker refused the two bodies of \library\ that did so (row~635
+of the revival's gap ledger).
+A rational number with the denominator zero is the quotient of a division by
+zero, and a division by zero whose result is an integer throws a
+\TYP{DivisionByZero} (\chapref{operators}); the Working Draft of February 2011 threw the same
+exception when a value \EXP{1/0} or \EXP{-1/0} was assigned to a variable of the
+rational type without the infinities (\secref{revival-literals}).
+Among the peers, Python's exact rational type refuses a zero denominator with a
+\texttt{ZeroDivisionError}, and its floor, ceiling and truncation of a
+floating-point infinity or NaN raise an error instead of returning a value.
+The full reasoning is in
+\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-slips/REPORT.md}
+in the revival's repository.
+\item[Effect] \Library\ throw \TYP{DivisionByZero} from \VAR{ceiling} and
+\VAR{truncate} at these three values, and so from \VAR{floor}, \VAR{round} and
+the two enclosing operators, which reach them; the interpreter runs them so.
+Before this change it returned the argument from all of them but \VAR{round},
+which stopped the program there.
+The compiled path's own library, used until the one library replaces it,
+declares no rational type.
+The floating-point types' rounding methods are not affected: they keep the
+floating-point type (row~330 of the revival's gap ledger).
+\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex},
+lines 479--481:
+\begin{quote}
+For types \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}},
+all of these methods simply return the argument if it is
+\EXP{+\infty}, \EXP{-\infty}, or \EXP{0/0}.
+\end{quote}
+\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
+A return to the original sentence would need the six methods and operators to
+declare a rational result, against their entries' \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, or would
+leave them returning a value outside the type they declare.
+\end{description}
+

\subsection{The rational trait}
\seclabel{revival-rationals}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{basic-rationals}.
\item[Change] The listing of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} extends \TYP{Number} in place of the
real numbers, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}, three instantiations of \TYP{Field} with
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}_{\neq}} as the multiplicative group,
\TYP{TotalOrderOperators} and \TYP{PartialOrderAndLattice}, and declares the
coercions from the five integer types, with a method entry for them.
The reciprocal, division and exponentiation return \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and so does
the absolute value; the four hyperfloor and hyperceiling operators return
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}}; the two comparisons by \OPR{CMP} become one, returning
\TYP{Comparison}.
The seventeen check methods leave the listing and the method entries.
Ten sentences of the method entries lose the words ``For types
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}},'' or ``For type
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}},'', the next word taking the capital (the sentence on
\OPR{MAXNUM} and \OPR{MINNUM} now begins ``The operators''); the parenthesis on the reciprocal's result type and
the sentence on \TYP{TotalComparison} are removed.
\item[Rationale] \secref{revival-numbers}.
A signature that named a refined type takes the type \library\ declare for the
method where they declare it (division and the absolute value return the
rational type, exponentiation by an integer returns it, and the comparison
\OPR{CMP} returns \TYP{Comparison}), and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} where
they do not.
The library declares \VAR{check} and \EXP{\VAR{check}^*} on \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, where
\secref{basic-rationals} states them, and no check by sign.
What the entries said of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} holds of
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, which holds their values.
\item[Effect] As \secref{revival-numbers}.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex}:
the listing's header, lines 177--183, and its lines 198--200, 206--207, 212,
222--225 and 228--244:
\begin{quote}
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait}\:\mathbb{Q}\)\\
{\tt~~~~}\(    \KWD{extends} \{\, \null\)\(\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{Q}^*,\)\\
{\tt~~~~~~~~~~~~~~}\(              \TYP{Field}\llbracket\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q}_{\neq},+,-,\cdot,/\rrbracket,\)\\
{\tt~~~~~~~~~~~~~~}\(              \TYP{Field}\llbracket\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q}_{\neq},+,-,\times,/\rrbracket,\)\\
{\tt~~~~~~~~~~~~~~}\(              \TYP{Field}\llbracket\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{Q}_{\neq},+,-,\KWD{juxtaposition},/\rrbracket,\)\\
{\tt~~~~~~~~~~~~~~}\(              \TYP{TotalOrderOperators}\llbracket\mathbb{Q},<,\leq,\geq,>,\OPR{CMP}\rrbracket,\)\\
{\tt~~~~~~~~~~~~~~}\(              \TYP{PartialOrderAndLattice}\llbracket\mathbb{Q},\leq,\OPR{MIN},\OPR{MAX}\rrbracket\,\}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} /(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Q}^*\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} /(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Q})\COLON \mathbb{Q}^{\#}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \mathord{\hbox{\tt\char'136}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{power}\COLON \mathbb{Z})\COLON \mathbb{Q}^{\#}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{CMP}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Q}^*)\COLON \TYP{TotalComparison}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{CMP}}(\KWD{self}, \VAR{other}\COLON \mathbb{Q}^{\#})\COLON \TYP{Comparison}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \left|\mathord{\KWD{self}}\right| \mathrel{\mathtt{:}}\:\mathbb{Q}_{\geq}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \lhfloor \mathord{\KWD{self}} \rhfloor\COLON \mathbb{N}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \lhceil \mathord{\KWD{self}} \rhceil\COLON \mathbb{N}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \lhhfloor \mathord{\KWD{self}} \rhhfloor\COLON \mathbb{N}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \KWD{opr} \lhhceil \mathord{\KWD{self}} \rhhceil\COLON \mathbb{N}\)\\
{\tt~~}\(  \VAR{check}(\KWD{self})\COLON \mathbb{Q} \KWD{throws}\:\TYP{CastError}\)\\
\subsection{Rational literals}
\seclabel{revival-literals}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{literals}.
\item[Change] \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} become one
type that includes \EXP{1/0}, \EXP{-1/0} and \EXP{0/0}; the run-time error on
assigning a \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} to a \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, the two ASCII names and the
reference to \secref{advanced-rationals} are removed, and the team's margin note
is kept.
\item[Rationale] \secref{revival-numbers}.
\item[Effect] As \secref{revival-numbers}.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex},
lines 188--209:
\begin{quote}
The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.

The type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ relaxes the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ and
includes two extra values, \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0} (sometimes called ``the
infinite rational'' and ``the indefinite rational'').
[The margin note of lines 193--197, kept unchanged in the revised text.]
If a value of type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ is assigned to a
variable of type $\mathbb{Q}$, a \TYP{DivisionByZero} is thrown
at run time if the value is \EXP{1/0} or \EXP{-1/0}.
The type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} includes all of \EXP{1/0}, \EXP{-1/0}, and
\EXP{0/0}.
The advantage of $\mathbb{Q}^{\#}$ is that it is closed under the rational
operations $+$, $-$, $\times$, and $/$.
In ASCII, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}, and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^\#} are written as \txt{QQ}, \txt{QQ\_star}, and
\txt{QQ\_splat}, respectively.
See \secref{advanced-rationals} for definitions of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*},
and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^\#}.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

content.content:
(* A mutable variable declared at the top level of a component, incremented
   inside `atomic do ... end` by the two implicit threads of a
   `do ... also do ... end`.

   Specification/basic/expressions/atomic.tex, section "Atomic Expressions" requires the read and the
   write of `counter` to appear to occur in a single atomic step with respect
   to any action of a thread dynamically outside, so the two threads together
   must perform exactly 2 * iterations increments.  atomic.tex, section "Atomic Expressions" gives the
   same shape as the chapter's own example: a loop body that reads and writes a
   shared counter inside `atomic`, which "will appear to occur atomically with
   respect to all other threads -- including both other iterations of the loop
   body".

   The increment is in a top-level function rather than written out in the loop
   body so that this program tests transaction membership alone; assignment
   from inside a nested code-generation context is the other half of the same
   repair and MutableTopLevelVarInLoop.fss covers it.

   Thread count.  A program in this corpus cannot set its own thread count:
   the count is read once from the environment (FORTRESS_THREADS,
   runtimeSystem/FortressExecutable.java:37-44) and Java cannot set an
   environment variable for its own process.  Nor does the gate set one: the
   fastTrack macro that runs compiler_tests sets FORTRESS_CACHES and no thread
   count (build.xml:927-953), and the harness runs each program in a
   subprocess that inherits the environment (FileTests.java:480-486), so the
   count is whatever the shell that started ant had.  explorations/experiment/env.sh:6
   exports FORTRESS_THREADS=1, and every run of this project is told to source
   it, so in practice this program runs at one worker and passes whether or
   not the implementation is correct.  The deterministic half of the repair,
   MutableTopLevelVarInLoop.fss, fails at one thread as well and is what
   carries the gate.  Runs both ways are in
   explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static/REPORT.md. *)

component AtomicTopLevelVar
export Executable

counter: ZZ32 := 0

iterations: ZZ32 = 20000

content.content:
Equality and inequality are not converted so: the declaration of \EXP{=} on
\TYP{Number} is applicable to an integer value and a numeral without coercion,
and so is the top-level declaration of \EXP{\neq}, whose parameters are of type
\TYP{Any}; the compiled type checker selects these and converts neither
operand, and \EXP{=} then compares the two as rationals, through the case for a
numeral that this change adds to \VAR{exactValue}, the function by which
\TYP{Number}'s \EXP{=} takes an exact value.
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} states in its api, for the same reason, the additive and
multiplicative operators its body declares.
\TYP{IntLiteral} declares its own \VAR{zero}, \VAR{one}, \VAR{even},
\VAR{odd}, \VAR{floor}, \VAR{ceiling}, \VAR{truncate}, \OPR{DIVIDES},
\OPR{TIMES} and a power with a numeral exponent, which a numeral reached
before as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, since no member of \TYP{Integral} is
applicable to a numeral of that type, even with coercion
(\secref{applicability-with-coercion}).
A numeral given where any integer type is accepted, as the count of a shift,
is converted to the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} that holds its value, as \secref{numeral-default} reads a
numeral whose conversions tie.
The interpreter still gives an integer numeral the type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value, so a numeral reaches none
----
\EXP{\TYP{ImmutableArray}\llbracket{}T, \mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}, with the
comment ``Replace ImmutableArray with ImmutableHeapSequence when
ImmutableHeapSequence is put into the libraries''
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Types.java}, lines
47--49, in the revival's repository), and the interpreter binds the parameter
to an immutable one-dimensional array of the arguments that the factory
\VAR{\_\_immutableFactory1} of \library\ builds
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/NonPrimitive.java},
lines 224--251), a value of that type.
The type is immutable, as the draft note asks.
Before this change the compiled type checker typed the parameter in the body
as \VAR{T}, the type of one argument, and read a parameter list with plain
bindings before a varargs binding as if the varargs binding were one more plain
